text:
Send every request to the cheapest model that passes. [curious] But passes what? Somebody has to write the test. And every model launch comes with a table of scores that looks like one. So what are those benchmarks measuring?

Each is a fixed set of questions with known answers. MMLU is multiple choice across fifty-seven subjects, from elementary math to law. GPQA Diamond is graduate science: PhDs from other fields, even with the web, score about thirty-four percent. SWE-bench hands over a real GitHub issue, and the patch has to pass the project's own tests. And Arc AGI asks for the rule behind a few grid puzzles, or in version three, the rules of a game, by playing it.

Reading a score starts with where it sits on the scale. On MMLU, ninety-two point three beats ninety-one point seven. But label errors cap that test near ninety-five. Six tenths of a point, that close to the ceiling, is noise. On Arc AGI three, sixty-two point seven against thirty point two, with room above both, is a real difference. That crowded ceiling is the first of four ways a launch table misleads.

One, saturation. Once everyone scores near the top, a test can't tell them apart. Every frontier model clears ninety-two on MMLU. GPQA Diamond, built to replace it, has its leaders around ninety-five. And tests fill up fast. Humanity's Last Exam went from every model under ten percent to the best near sixty, in twenty months. The tell: if every model in a row sits within three points, skip the row.
